sources.title: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field
sources.note: Three experiments with over 80,000 unique users on one German website. Notice placement and choice structure affected behaviour. The setting limits generalisation.

sources.title: ‘Okay, whatever’: An Evaluation of Cookie Consent Interfaces
sources.note: 191-interface inspection and a 1,109-participant experiment. Supports evaluating awareness, preferred decisions and usability as well as consent rates.

sources.note: Defines gamification through game-design elements in non-game contexts. A definition is not proof of user benefit.

slides.title: Cookie Homes
slides.cue: A working interaction prototype and a testable research question
slides.script: Good morning. I am Lee Chen Xuan, and my project is Cookie Homes, a gamified interface for understanding cookie choices. I will explain the problem, show how the prototype addresses it, and describe how I plan to test whether the interface helps users. The interaction prototype is implemented. User benefit and consent write-back remain work to evaluate and complete.
slides.watch: State the current stage immediately. Do not imply that user testing is complete.
slides.transition: First, consider the decision that appears before a user can continue browsing.

slides.title: Why is it so complicated?
slides.cue: A choice can be available without being easy to understand
slides.script: This screenshot from the report illustrates a familiar situation: a visitor wants to use a website and encounters privacy choices. The visitor may understand that cookies exist, yet still struggle to connect terms such as functional or targeting cookies with a practical consequence. Opening a preference centre gives more control, but also requires attention and interpretation. My concern is the quality of that decision: can users understand the request and express what they want? A screenshot alone cannot establish that a particular design manipulates users, or that everyone finds it difficult. It gives the real-world context. The next slide provides empirical evidence that design can affect consent behaviour. For this project, the initial intended audience is adult web users with limited familiarity with cookie terminology. Recruitment criteria and prior knowledge will need to be recorded in the study.
slides.watch: The FIFA image is an example from the report, not evidence of a violation or a current live-site audit.
slides.transition: Research gives a stronger basis for the problem than personal impressions of a banner.

slides.title: Design affects consent decisions
slides.cue: Three studies establish the design problem
slides.script: Nouwens and colleagues found a 22 to 23 percentage-point increase in consent when they removed the opt-out option from the first page, in a field experiment with 40 participants. That result concerns a specific design change and sample. Utz and colleagues studied more than 80,000 unique users on one German website and also found that notice placement and choice structure affected behaviour. Habib and colleagues examined usability through a 1,109-participant experiment, including how visible choices were and whether people could make their preferred decision. Together, these studies support treating consent as an interaction-design problem. They do not show that games or chatbots solve it. My proposed response is therefore a design hypothesis that must be tested. The outcome I care about is whether a person understands the request and can express their intended choice, rather than simply whether the person accepts fewer or more cookies.
slides.watch: Say percentage points. Keep all sample sizes attached to the correct studies. Do not generalise the effect size to every website.
slides.transition: That evidence leads to a more precise problem statement.

slides.title: Problem statement and project scope
slides.cue: Understanding and faithful expression are the target outcomes
slides.script: The problem I address is that users may struggle to understand cookie purposes and translate their intentions into consent choices. Cookie Homes investigates whether contextual explanations and a gamified journey can help with that step. I define success in terms of understanding, agreement with the user's expressed intent, and the effort required. The initial technical scope is a local prototype with a Chrome connector and Cookiebot-oriented inputs. I am not claiming to identify every tracker or replace all privacy controls. Cookie consent is only one part of online privacy. This scope makes the project manageable and gives us a clear basis for evaluating the interaction before broadening compatibility. A useful result could be that some features help while others add effort. That would guide the final design.
slides.watch: Use a narrow, testable problem. Avoid saying that all users are confused or all banners are deceptive.
slides.transition: Even within this scope, there are several design challenges.

slides.title: Why the problem is challenging
slides.cue: Clarity must preserve meaning and intent
slides.script: There are four connected challenges. First, an analogy can simplify a request while accidentally changing its meaning. A friendly guest should not imply that a cookie is harmless. Second, metadata does not prove purpose, and a public declaration can be missing or inaccurate. Third, a question such as 'Is this tracking me?' is not a decision to accept or reject. The interface needs to distinguish questions, uncertainty and explicit choices. Fourth, engagement only matters if it supports the consent task. A more enjoyable experience could still be slower or more confusing. These challenges explain why the project needs both technical safeguards and user evaluation. The design should help users make decisions, while making uncertainty visible and allowing mistakes to be corrected.
slides.watch: Do not equate a pleasant experience with informed consent.
slides.transition: Existing work addresses different parts of this same process.

slides.title: Related work and our contribution
slides.cue: Connect consent design, enforcement and conversation
slides.script: I position the project alongside three strands of work. Consent-interface studies establish that presentation can affect behaviour and usability. CookieBlock addresses purpose classification and enforcement: it predicts categories and removes cookies according to configured preferences. That is closely related to my cookie-data pipeline, but its central contribution differs from studying how people understand requests and express preferences. PriBot provides prior work on answering privacy-policy questions in natural language, so conversational privacy assistance is not a new idea by itself. Cookie Homes combines a contextual home-and-guest representation, conversation and visible decision feedback into a particular interaction that can be evaluated. The contribution is the design, its implementation, and evidence about its benefits and limitations. I do not claim to invent cookie management, chatbots or gamification.
slides.watch: CookieBlock uses machine learning for purpose classification. Cookie Homes uses AI for language interpretation. Keep those roles distinct.
slides.transition: The research gap needs to be stated at the level that these comparisons support.

slides.title: Research gap and research questions
slides.cue: A scoped evaluation gap, not a claim of being the first
slides.script: The reviewed work does not establish whether this particular gamified consent journey improves understanding and preserves intended choices relative to a clear conventional interface. That is the evaluation gap I propose to address. My primary question is whether the complete interface helps users understand cookie purposes without reducing agreement with their intended choices or adding unacceptable effort. A secondary question asks which elements help or hinder: the analogy, scenarios, conversational support and progress feedback. Comparing the complete interface with a dashboard can evaluate the overall package, but it cannot isolate every component. If feasible, I will add a focused comparison with fixed-choice scenario cards to examine the additional contribution of conversation. A broader literature search is still needed before making any claim of novelty across the entire field.
slides.watch: Say 'this particular journey' and 'reviewed work'. Do not claim that no gamified privacy interface exists.
slides.transition: Here is how the proposed interaction makes a cookie request concrete.

slides.title: The home and guest analogy
slides.cue: Use a concrete request while keeping technical evidence accessible
slides.script: A website becomes a home, and a cookie becomes a guest with a request. For example, a guest who keeps a settings notebook represents a request to remember preferences. The user can inspect what that request means, ask a question and decide whether to allow it. The mapping is an explanation layer over the available evidence. A guest is not a real person, and a cookie does not itself have human intentions. Technical details must remain accessible so the analogy can be checked. The gamified elements are a narrative setting, a sequence of scenario tasks, progress feedback and visible consequences for choices. These are intended to encourage attention to the decision. They should not reward a particular privacy answer. Their benefit remains a hypothesis, and the study should also check whether people misunderstand the metaphor or feel pressured to complete the journey.
slides.watch: A cookie is a stored record. Avoid implying that it independently watches, thinks or has intentions.
slides.transition: Each feature needs a reason to exist and a measurable benefit.

slides.title: How each feature addresses the problem
slides.cue: Every feature has a proposed benefit to test
slides.script: This table connects the design to the problem. The analogy aims to make purpose easier to explain. Concrete scenarios help users relate an abstract category to a practical request. Conversation supports questions and clarification when a user cannot express a choice through a simple control. Progress and visible outcomes show what has been decided, while evidence and uncertainty labels show what is not known. These are proposed mechanisms, not measured improvements. For example, if participants enjoy the guest story but score no better on comprehension, enjoyment alone would not support the main claim. Likewise, if conversation feels natural but produces incorrect changes, that feature needs revision. I will use task measures and participants' explanations to identify which parts contribute value. This also gives me a basis for simplifying the design when a feature adds little.
slides.watch: Do not read every table cell. Walk through one example and summarise the remaining rows.
slides.transition: The chatbot deserves particular scrutiny because it adds both flexibility and risk.

slides.title: Why use an AI chatbot?
slides.cue: Contextual questions and language variation justify testing AI
slides.script: The reason for exploring an AI chatbot is that users may describe intentions in everyday language or ask an unexpected follow-up question. For example, a user may say 'Remember my settings, but do not personalise advertisements.' The system needs to connect that message to the relevant requests and distinguish it from uncertainty. A scripted interface could handle a small set of predictable questions, and fixed controls remain a serious alternative. AI is only useful if the added flexibility improves the task enough to justify latency, interpretation errors and external processing. In this prototype, the model proposes structured decisions. A separate rules engine validates allowed categories, targets and actions before changing local state. That separation constrains the action space, but a structurally valid decision can still misunderstand the user. A comparison against fixed-choice scenarios is therefore useful, together with review and correction before future website write-back.
slides.watch: Do not say AI is necessary or guarantees understanding. Explain the alternative and the test.
slides.transition: The architecture shows where interpretation ends and state changes begin.

slides.title: Prototype architecture
slides.cue: Separate evidence, interpretation, validation and enforcement
slides.script: Read the diagram across the top row and then back along the lower row. The extension collects browser metadata, the site's Cookiebot consent state and available public declaration rows. The adapter normalises those records and matches purpose evidence. Cookie Homes turns the result into scenarios that the user can inspect and discuss. Chat requests go through the local server to Gemini, which returns a reply and proposed structured decisions. The rules engine checks the supported actions before updating the local guest state and summary. The dashed block is planned work: a review step and an integration that applies supported choices to the site's CMP. That distinction matters. Moving a guest in the prototype currently changes the application state, not the website's cookie permissions. The diagram also makes the external data flow explicit. Running the application on localhost does not mean every part of processing stays on the device.
slides.watch: Point to the dashed block. Say clearly that current guest changes do not enforce website consent.
slides.transition: The three input sources answer different questions and should not be conflated.

slides.title: Where the cookie information comes from
slides.cue: Metadata, consent state and purpose evidence are separate
slides.script: Browser cookie metadata comes from the Chrome cookies API. It describes records currently visible within the extension's permitted scope, including names, domains and expiry attributes. The Cookiebot snapshot comes from selected fields of window.Cookiebot in the webpage's JavaScript context. It describes the current category-level consent state. The extension serialises those fields into JSON; it does not download a private Cookiebot database. Public declaration pages provide cookie-purpose descriptions and categories where available. The website loads the Cookiebot SDK from its service, but the object we read is the object currently in that page. These sources have limits. A declared cookie may not currently be stored, and a stored cookie is not proof that the current visit created it. The browser API returns records that can include values, but our connector excludes those values from the payload it sends onward. Missing or ambiguous purpose matches remain unclassified.
slides.watch: Say cookie values are excluded from onward payloads. Do not claim the browser API never exposes values to extension code.
slides.transition: These components support the interaction prototype that is available today.

slides.title: What the prototype can do today
slides.cue: Implemented interaction, incomplete end-to-end integration
slides.script: The current prototype has three main capabilities. It collects and normalises available site inputs through the extension connector. It represents cookie requests through the home-and-guest journey. It interprets chat and updates local decisions through the rules engine. The interface includes purpose details, uncertainty handling, progress and an outcome summary. This is enough to demonstrate the interaction concept and prepare controlled tasks. The next implementation steps include moving the journey into an extension view and adding verified consent write-back. User evaluation is also still planned. I will avoid presenting a percentage-complete estimate because the remaining research and integration work cannot be measured reliably by counting features. Instead, I separate implemented components, unvalidated behaviour and planned work. The demo will focus on the current local decision flow.
slides.watch: Code-level checks do not establish user benefit, full browser coverage or live-model accuracy.
slides.transition: I will demonstrate a clear choice and a case that requires clarification.

slides.title: Live demonstration
slides.cue: Show evidence, a clear choice and a clarification
slides.script: I will first show the input evidence and explain whether I am using the live connector or a prepared fixture. Next, I will open one home and select a guest so the purpose and technical details are visible. I will make a clear choice and point to the exact change in the local state and summary. Then I will use an uncertain reply to demonstrate the intended clarification behaviour. If the model changes a choice incorrectly, I will identify that as an interpretation failure rather than describe it as expected behaviour. Finally, I will show how a choice can be revised in the local journey. Throughout the demonstration, the website's actual consent remains unchanged because write-back is not implemented. If the API or network fails, I will use the screenshot on the previous slide to explain the flow and state that the live response is unavailable. The planned evaluation must test these behaviours systematically, beyond a successful demonstration.
slides.watch: Rehearse exact prompts on the selected guest. The demo is an example, not an accuracy benchmark. Do not expose keys, personal messages or unrelated tabs.
slides.transition: The demo also shows why the safeguards and remaining limitations matter.

slides.title: Safeguards and remaining limitations
slides.cue: A valid action can still be a mistaken interpretation
slides.script: Some protections are already in the implementation. Structured actions must name supported categories and valid guest targets. The rules engine protects guests labelled essential. When the model flags a response as ambiguous, the server clears the proposed decisions. Unmatched purposes remain visibly unclassified, and their local choices cannot become a general unknown-purpose preference. These controls do not make the system infallible. The model could fail to recognise ambiguity, a source could label a cookie incorrectly, or a valid action could target the wrong user intention. Review before external write-back, recovery, privacy notices and broader reliability testing remain necessary. The local test suite currently has eleven passes and two failures, involving an older unknown-purpose rule and an older guest label. Those expectations need reconciliation with the intended behaviour. I should not describe the full prototype as validated until the discrepancies and relevant end-to-end checks are resolved.
slides.watch: Clarification depends partly on model behaviour. Essential protection relies on classification. Do not claim either eliminates all risk.
slides.transition: The design alternatives make these trade-offs explicit.

slides.title: Design alternatives and trade-offs
slides.cue: The simplest successful interface should remain an option
slides.script: I considered three main interfaces. A clear category dashboard is familiar and relatively easy to implement, although users still need to understand its labels. Fixed-choice scenario cards keep the contextual explanation while avoiding language interpretation. The selected conversational journey supports questions and flexible expression, but adds processing time and error risk. These are alternatives worth comparing, rather than options that can be dismissed before testing. The first study should include a competent, neutral baseline with the same information. If fixed cards perform as well as chat with less effort, that would be a reason to simplify the design or make conversation optional. The same logic applies to the analogy: its value depends on whether it improves the user's task, rather than its visual appeal alone.
slides.watch: Use a fair baseline. Comparing only with a deliberately poor banner would weaken the conclusion.
slides.transition: The study design needs to separate a useful interface from a merely novel experience.

slides.title: Planned user evaluation
slides.cue: Compare the whole interface fairly and isolate components cautiously
slides.script: I propose a small pilot followed by a controlled task-based study. The core comparison is Cookie Homes against a clear category dashboard, using equivalent purpose information and matched tasks. Where practical, participants will try both interfaces, with the order counterbalanced and different but equivalent scenarios to limit learning effects. I will record prior familiarity with cookies. For choice fidelity, scripted tasks can provide known target decisions. Personal preference tasks can compare the interface result with a direct statement, followed by confirmation and an explanation of any change. A questionnaire is only a reference, not perfect ground truth, because learning may legitimately change a preference. If resources permit, fixed-choice scenario cards provide an additional comparison for the chatbot. A comparison of two complete interfaces cannot establish which individual feature caused an effect. Recruitment, sample size, primary outcomes and analysis will be specified with the supervisor before the main study, following the required institutional review.
slides.watch: The protocol is proposed. Do not invent a final participant count or imply that approval has already been obtained.
slides.transition: These are the outcomes that would support or challenge the design.

slides.title: Evaluation metrics and success criteria
slides.cue: Prioritise understanding and faithful decisions over acceptance rates
slides.script: The primary outcomes are comprehension and choice fidelity. Comprehension questions should check purposes and consequences in plain language, ideally including a new example to test transfer beyond memorising the story. Choice fidelity measures whether the captured result matches an explicit task intention or a participant-confirmed preference. I will record unintended changes and correctly handled clarification separately. Secondary measures include completion, time, perceived effort, confidence and engagement. Technical checks cover uncertainty labels, supported actions and eventually the observed result of write-back. Numerical targets and analysis decisions should be set before the main study, with effect estimates and uncertainty reported. A higher acceptance or rejection rate is not itself success. If engagement increases while understanding declines or mistakes increase, that would not support the main objective. A null or negative result is still useful if it identifies which design choices should be removed or revised.
slides.watch: An absence of observed errors in a small sample is not a guarantee of zero risk.
slides.transition: The work plan prioritises a bounded implementation and a credible evaluation.

slides.title: Planned work and feasibility
slides.cue: Finish one supported path before broadening coverage
slides.script: The plan is organised around dependencies. First, agree the baseline and study protocol, reconcile current test expectations and investigate the write-back path. Then move the journey into an extension view and implement review plus the supported Cookiebot integration. Pilot sessions should expose usability, accessibility and reliability problems before the main study. The later stages are data collection, analysis, refinement and the final report. The initial scope remains one browser and one CMP. Broader CMP coverage, comprehensive purpose classification and privacy profiling are outside the core deliverable. If reliable write-back is blocked, the fallback is a clear hand-off to the site's controls and an evaluation of preference expression. I would then narrow the final claim to decision support and report the integration limitation explicitly. The essential output is a demonstrable prototype and credible evidence about the interaction.
slides.watch: The schedule is provisional and refers to next-semester weeks. Do not claim consent write-back is already solved by finding an API method.
slides.transition: The project can now be summarised as a specific question with an implemented test vehicle.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.cue: A defensible problem, an implemented approach and an evaluation plan
slides.script: The literature establishes that consent-interface design can influence decisions and usability. Cookie Homes responds with an implemented home-and-guest journey that combines contextual explanations, questions and visible local choices. Its value to users is still a hypothesis. The next stage is to complete the supported integration and compare the interaction with a clear baseline. The central question is whether it improves understanding while preserving intended choices at an acceptable level of effort. That gives the project a concrete contribution even if the findings show that some features should be simplified. Thank you. I welcome questions about the scope, design trade-offs and evaluation.
slides.watch: End on the research question. Do not conclude that the solution already improves informed consent.
slides.transition: Questions.

slides.title: Thank you
slides.cue: Questions and discussion
slides.script: Pause and let the evaluator finish the question. Give the direct answer first, state the relevant evidence or limitation, and explain the next test or implementation step. Use the backup slides only when they help answer the question.
slides.watch: Avoid rushing into a defence before understanding the objection.

slides.title: Backup: consent write-back and granularity
slides.cue: Category controls limit per-cookie enforcement
slides.script: Cookiebot documents category-level submitCustomConsent for preferences, statistics and marketing. That creates a candidate integration path, not proof that the extension already writes consent correctly. The prototype currently captures guest-level local choices, while a CMP may expose only category-level controls. Conflicting choices within a category must therefore be shown to the user and resolved explicitly. I should not silently convert them into a category choice or claim per-cookie control that the CMP does not provide. The integration needs active-site checks, a review step, execution in the supported context and read-back of the resulting consent state. Updating the CMP state also does not prove that every tracker complied. Where this cannot be verified, the interface should report the limitation and offer the site's controls.
slides.watch: Read-back verifies CMP state; broader network or storage testing is needed to assess site behaviour.

slides.title: Backup: threats to study validity
slides.cue: Prevent confounds and limit the conclusions
slides.script: The major validity threats are learning effects, novelty, unequal information, a weak baseline, prior privacy knowledge and demand effects. Counterbalancing and equivalent tasks reduce some of these problems. Participants should receive the same substantive cookie information and enough time to use each interface. Objective questions and task outcomes should supplement self-reported liking. Personal preferences can change with understanding, so an initial questionnaire should not be treated as an immutable correct answer. A small convenience sample supports exploratory findings and error discovery rather than claims about all web users. Evaluating the complete design does not isolate the effect of the chatbot or game elements. Those claims need a component comparison or should remain open questions.
slides.watch: Explain which threat each design choice addresses and what remains unresolved.

slides.title: Backup: data flow and technical limits
slides.cue: Local application, external interpretation and limited evidence
slides.script: The connector excludes cookie values from the input payload, but it still handles metadata and purpose descriptions. Chat requests include user messages, recent context and relevant guest information, which the local server can send to Gemini. Participants need a clear explanation of this flow, data minimisation and a defined retention policy before testing. Public declaration text is untrusted input and should be bounded and treated as evidence, not instructions. Structural validation reduces the action surface but does not fully solve prompt injection or semantic mistakes. The current prototype needs broader adversarial and integration tests. Browser permissions, absent declarations, inaccessible SDK state and unsupported sites must produce visible limitations rather than fabricated certainty. A service outage should leave choices unchanged and present a recoverable error.
slides.watch: Do not promise local-only processing or claim that stripping cookie values removes all privacy risks.

slides.title: References: consent and related systems
slides.cue: Sources for the problem and technical comparison
slides.script: These papers support the consent-design problem and the comparison with CookieBlock. Use the relevant source when answering a question. Do not treat their findings as results from Cookie Homes.
slides.watch: Retain study contexts and sample sizes when quoting findings.

slides.title: References: interaction and integration
slides.cue: Sources for conversational support, game elements and APIs
slides.script: These sources establish prior conversational work, a definition of gamification, human-AI interaction guidance and the documented Cookiebot interface. They motivate design choices and candidate integration mechanisms. They do not establish the effectiveness or reliability of the current prototype.
slides.watch: Cookiebot documentation describes an interface contract; test the actual integration.
